À la French est un rendez-vous hebdomada: À la French is a weekly tech conversation run by three people who have built things: Jean-Baptiste Kempf, president of VideoLAN and the man who carried VLC to become one of the most downloaded pieces of software in history — formerly at Shadow and Scaleway, and who refused to monetise VLC while everyone around him was raising money; Steeve Morin, entrepreneur and mobile expert; and Mehdi Medjaoui, founder of APIdays, the global festival dedicated to APIs.
Three words, two languages, one agenda. The name is both a wink and a thesis: France produced VLC, the Minitel, Dassault Systèmes, BlaBlaCar, Ledger, Mistral AI — and there's no reason "talking tech" and "talking French" should be at odds. The format is simple: three experts break down tech news and host people who actually build things — CTOs, researchers, engineers. Topics range from AI — architecture decisions and cost models, not headlines — to open source, digital sovereignty, infrastructure and tech geopolitics.
Dans beaucoup de podcasts tech, on perfo: In many tech podcasts, people perform mastery, vision, expertise. Here, nobody performs. JB Kempf says "I don't know" when he doesn't know, "it's complicated" when it is, "we got it wrong" when they got it wrong. In a space where everyone tries to sound like a visionary, this intellectual honesty is almost subversive.
C'est ce qui change tout. Quand un CTO v: That's what changes everything. When a CTO comes to explain their architecture, they don't need to simplify so as not to lose the host: they can go deep, and the host follows — then goes further. Extremely rare in French-language tech podcasting.
Pas numéro deux, pas dans le top dix. Sa: Not number two, not top ten. With no marketing campaign or controversy: a launch at the APIdays conference, some buzz, the YouTube algorithm noticing, and the top spot among French-language tech podcasts. A sign that an audience was waiting for exactly this and didn't have it yet.
Alex portait cet épisode, et il a ouvert: Alex carried this episode, and he opened by defusing the criticism himself: he knows Jean-Baptiste Kempf personally, met him at a podcast party and invited him to his company. "I'm a fan and I own it." The bias is declared, not hidden — it's up to the listener to factor it in. Still, the conclusion holds without the friendship: À la French answers a question nobody else was tackling in French — what a conversation sounds like between people who have built important things, have nothing left to prove, and speak freely about what they see coming.
Deux limites, réelles. Le format n'est p: Two real limits. The format isn't accessible: without a technical background, some episodes leave you on the platform, and that can be intimidating. And the risk of three strong co-hosts materialises — discussions sometimes head in every direction at once. It's lively, but not always easy to follow. The comparison with Micode's Underscore_, reviewed in our episode 42, clarifies the split: Micode makes tech desirable for everyone, À la French discusses it among peers. It's the difference between a very good documentary about jazz and a jam session at midnight — both are worth the trip, you just don't wear the same shoes.
Sur leur promesse, en revanche, ils sont: On their promise, though, they're flawless: they wanted to create the tech show tech people dreamed of having in France. They created it. And the sovereignty question — what would we do if the United States or China banned their technologies for us? — has never been so present in companies' daily lives.
